## Why This Is Asked

This tests precise bit manipulation skills for rearranging 8-byte blocks without loops, essential for portable endianness handling in systems programming.

## Key Concepts

- Byte-level masking with 64-bit constants
- Multi-stage shuffles to minimize operations
- Endianness portability across platforms

## Code Example

```c
uint64_t bswap64(uint64_t x) {
  x = ((x & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL) << 8) | ((x >> 8) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FFULL);
  x = ((x & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL) << 16) | ((x >> 16) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFFULL);
  return (x << 32) | (x >> 32);
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify correctness of this implementation?
- What are the trade-offs between this approach and using built-in byte swap functions?
- How would this differ on a little-endian vs big-endian system?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to implement a rotation primitive with wrap-around using only shifts and masks, including masking to handle large r and the n=0 edge case.

## Key Concepts
- Circular shift using (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n))
- Masking r with 31 to confine to 0..31
- Edge-case n=0 preserves x exactly

## Code Example
```c
static inline uint32_t rotl32(uint32_t x, unsigned r) {
  unsigned n = r & 31; // 0..31
  return (x << n) | (x >> (32 - n));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you generalize to 64-bit rotates?
- What are the potential performance differences vs. compiler intrinsics like _rotl?
- How would you test across boundary values (r=0, r=31, r=32, r=33)?
